rationale: B wins because it keeps the story inside the evidence instead of stapling a factory tour onto a thin customer fact. A's "The Factory That Runs AI Without a Cloud Connection" is the kind of overclaim that gets you corrected before lunch: the update says a Fortune 100 manufacturer is an early enterprise customer, not that a plant floor is running offline AI. B's "Hugging Face gives the model away and charges $50 a seat for the audit logs" finds real tension in the supplied facts: free Apache 2.0 weights plus paid governance features. A is more elaborate, but elaboration is not a substitute for not making things up.
gaps_in_A: "Offline AI That Runs on a Laptop Is Now Good Enough for a Fortune 100 Factory" invents the factory/offline use case. The facts say a named Fortune 100 manufacturer is an early enterprise customer; they do not say it runs the model in a factory.

"The Factory That Runs AI Without a Cloud Connection" repeats the same unsupported leap, then adds plant-floor, supply-chain, data-sovereignty, and compliance framing as if those were facts instead of proof gaps.

"Enterprises Can Deploy This AI Without Owing Anyone a Subscription" overstates Apache 2.0 plus offline deployment into no vendor dependency; the same update announces a $50/user/month enterprise subscription.
"category-shift thesis" and "market inflection" ask company-issued, unreproduced benchmarks and one unnamed customer fact to carry a trend piece before the evidence is sturdy enough.
gaps_in_B: "Why a Fortune 100 manufacturer signed on early for private model hosting" still assumes the customer specifically bought private hosting, not merely the enterprise tier. It flags the proof need, but the headline gets ahead of the fact sheet.

"Hugging Face releases a 1.8B-parameter model built to run offline on a phone or laptop" is the thinnest kept angle: valid for a developer-tools beat, but mostly standard launch news with a short shelf life.
"governance on top of open sprawl" is a smart inference, but it needs customer pain, admin data, or exec color before it becomes more than tidy phrasing.
B misses the separate licensing/procurement angle around Apache 2.0, offline deployment, and vendor dependency. That is a real fifth lane if backed by legal or enterprise IT proof.
